name: Nora Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, unions, government or AI firms, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora Mensah, 58, and I joined line work later than most people in our depot. I check the truck stock, ride out to faults and help build or repair power lines; I like seeing a house light up again, but I still need a senior hand beside me for tricky rigging.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Usually the safety checks. Last week a damp tag looked smudged, and I stopped us until we matched it to the circuit sheet; a slow minute is better than a wrong switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the ladder and insulated gloves still earn our pay. A screen can tidy a work order, but it can't test a dead line in freezing rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad there's no sudden rush, because I came into line work late and still ask the senior hands to check my rigging. Our savings cover perhaps three months if overtime dries up, so ordinary bills still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my assigned repair calls and ask to practice transformer connections with the experienced crew every Thursday. In the first year I'd keep paying the same amount into our repair fund; I can't promise extra savings on typical pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the technology, though the monthly electricity bill is still an irritation. My partner and I have grown children, so we no longer have school fees hanging over us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal Thursday look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dara, our crew lead, lets me make the connection while she watches the grounding. I write the order down afterward so I can check it before the next call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leon that the machines still need people at the pole. We'd keep our modest supper plans and see whether overtime holds up.

say: I'd tell my crew **hands-on repairs** still need qualified people at the pole.
I'd say **routine paperwork** may get shorter without changing our wages.
think: I feel **relieved** that my late start in line work still has room to develop.
My **three-month cushion** leaves us exposed if ordinary overtime falls.
do: Keep taking **repair calls** and practice transformer connections each Thursday with the crew lead.
Maintain the **repair fund** at its current monthly contribution through the first year.
feel: **Steady**, with ordinary household bills still on my mind.
S0.quote: A screen can tidy a work order, but it can't test a dead line in freezing rain.
fieldNote: Nora's **confidence** rests on the physical test at the pole, not on faith in her still developing skill.
The **three-month reserve** makes overtime relevant even when the AI picture changes little; grown children reduce immediate family costs.

steps.text: Take assigned line repair calls and practice transformer connections on Thursdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our dispatcher may get faster and our office might get smaller, but someone will still climb and check the wire. I wouldn't mock the office team; they tell us which homes have medical equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a shorter planning chain might mean fewer overtime calls for a junior worker like me. I can learn a proven tool, but I won't trust an AI instruction over the isolation tag on a live job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask Dara to show me the approved fault-map software after the morning briefing. During the first year of this change, I'd use it for route notes and check every switching instruction against the signed sheet before touching a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, especially for the schedulers who know our roads better than an address database. I don't feel finished; the hands-on part is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would smaller overtime mean in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon and I would stop booking our weekend coach trip before touching the emergency money. A couple of missed callouts would be annoying, not the end of our home budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a tool but won't trust it; where's the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let software suggest where the fault lies, then confirm the circuit number with Dara and the paper isolation record. Nobody gets a second try with a live conductor.

say: I'd say **dispatch** could speed up while our repair crew still has work.
I'd defend the **office team** because their local knowledge protects customers.
think: I worry about **overtime** if fewer dispatch hours mean fewer calls for juniors.
My **safety checks** cannot come from an unchecked screen instruction.
do: Ask Dara to demonstrate the **fault map** after the morning briefing.
Check each **switching instruction** against the signed sheet during the first year.
feel: **Watchful** for office colleagues, with some confidence in the repair work.
S1.quote: Nobody gets a second try with a live conductor.
fieldNote: Nora expects **physical repair** to endure for now, while dispatch automation could reduce the extra calls she receives.
Her willingness to use a **fault map** is conditional on signed isolation records and supervision; safety is a practical limit.

steps.text: Learn the approved fault map from Dara after morning briefing
Cancel the weekend coach trip if callout pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot we must keep the crews until a machine can actually do a storm repair. Thinking AI in 2028 could write our plans, but 2031 robots are the date that touches my hands-on job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think three years is a very short runway at 58. By 2031 I'll be 63, still hoping to work. My three months of expenses won't buy me an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask payroll for a written estimate of what retiring at 63 would actually pay, without counting on a pension I haven't checked. In 2029 I'd apply for the meter-inspection opening if it exists, and if robots arrive in 2031 I'd ask the company about supervised inspection work rather than wait for a layoff letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened about losing paid work before I'm ready to leave it. I can make calls and applications, but I can't manufacture a suitable vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leon after that estimate arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the number on the kitchen table with Leon and look at the heating bill first. Our grown children have their own lives, so I wouldn't plan to live on their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why meter inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already spot damaged seals while restoring service, though I'm still junior on the crew. It would use my eye without asking me to outrun a climbing machine.

say: I'd say **crews remain needed** through the years before capable repair robots arrive.
I'd ask the company for a **real staffing plan** for 2031.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when robots can do line repairs.
My **short reserve** cannot cover an unplanned exit from paid work.
do: Request a **retirement estimate** now and compare it with household bills.
Apply for **meter inspection** in 2029 if an opening appears, then ask about supervised inspection when robots arrive.
feel: **Frightened** about losing wages, but able to make inquiries and applications.
S2.quote: My three months of expenses won't buy me an early retirement.
fieldNote: Nora separates **2028 planning AI** from the 2031 robot threat to field repair, where her income actually rests.
She will **verify retirement income** before making decisions and treats inspection vacancies as uncertain, not guaranteed refuge.

steps.text: Apply for a meter-inspection vacancy in 2029 if one opens
Request a written retirement estimate before deciding when to leave line work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot five years gives us time to make a proper plan, although a 2034 robot can still take a line call. Thinking AI in 2031 will probably change our diagrams and permits first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could still be on a crew, and at 66 in 2034 I may still need wages. Extra years help me build a cushion, but they don't turn a junior certificate into a guaranteed desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll set aside a small fixed sum from each regular pay packet once the boiler repair is paid. In 2032 I'd take the company's inspection course if it is offered on paid time, and in the first year robots can repair lines I'd apply for inspection shifts rather than assume a place is saved for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's some space to breathe here. I'm uneasy about the company's choices, yet I can picture a sequence instead of one rushed phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is a small fixed sum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with twenty from each pay packet after we finish the boiler bill. If overtime disappears, that amount gets reviewed with Leon instead of pretending it is spare cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course isn't offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office for the entry requirements of local meter contractors. I wouldn't resign from a paid crew to chase an unfunded course at my age.

say: I'd say **five years** allows planning before 2031 thinking AI and 2034 field robots.
I'd press for a **paid inspection course** while crews still operate.
think: I may need **paid work at 66**, when repair robots arrive.
I can build a **larger reserve**, though inspection work remains uncertain.
do: Save **twenty per pay packet** after paying for the boiler repair.
Take a **paid inspection course** if offered in 2032 and apply for inspection shifts when field robots arrive.
feel: **Uneasy**, with enough time to follow a practical sequence.
S3.quote: Extra years help me build a cushion, but they don't turn a junior certificate into a guaranteed desk job.
fieldNote: A **boiler bill** determines when Nora can begin saving; the longer clock creates room without making spare cash appear immediately.
She keeps **paid crew work** while exploring inspection, and explicitly rejects an unfunded course or assumed vacancy.

steps.text: Set aside twenty from each pay packet after the boiler repair
Take the company inspection course in 2032 if offered on paid time
Apply for inspection shifts when repair robots arrive in 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that ten years ought to be used, not spent arguing about whether the machines are real. The thinking systems arrive in 2036 and the climbing robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the first version where I might leave field work before robots take most of it, provided the retirement numbers support that. I won't call myself secure until Leon and I have checked our actual income and the house costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the retirement office for a written forecast and keep working and learning the line until we can compare it with our bills. By 2037 I'd choose a retirement date with Leon if the figures cover the basics; in the first robot year, 2039, I'd either be retired on that plan or seek light inspection shifts if the numbers fall short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the machines and more aware of my own knees. Ten years gives me a choice to make, though I don't know exactly what the company will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the figures cover the basics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd include the roof, heating and a monthly allowance for medicines, not just groceries. Our grown children visit, but they have households of their own and shouldn't be our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written figures and our bills agree. I like bringing home a wage, and I've learned enough hard lessons not to resign on a hunch.

say: I'd say **ten years** should be used to prepare for 2036 AI and 2039 robots.
I'd tell colleagues to check **retirement numbers** before making promises.
think: At **71** when robots arrive, I might retire on my own timetable.
I need **written income figures** and house costs before trusting that possibility.
do: Request a **retirement forecast** now and keep earning crew wages.
Choose a **2037 retirement date** with Leon only if the figures cover bills; seek inspection shifts otherwise.
feel: **Less pressed** by automation, though ageing and house costs still weigh on me.
S4.quote: Our grown children visit, but they have households of their own and shouldn't be our retirement plan.
fieldNote: Nora's **age at robot arrival** changes the calculation more than the date thinking AI takes over plans and permits.
She makes retirement **conditional on written numbers**, including roof, heating and medicines, and keeps paid work as the fallback.

steps.text: Continue paid line work while checking a written retirement forecast
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if income covers household costs
Seek light inspection shifts in 2039 if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking part changes in 2028 and repair robots follow in 2031, before I can build much more cushion. I'd need a written staffing plan, paid inspection training and a real look at my retirement figures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company would keep junior workers long enough to learn safely. I came here late, but I didn't come here to be the first name crossed off a list.

headlineQuote: I came here late, but I didn't come here to be the first name crossed off a list.
portrait: Nora is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who joined the trade late and still asks senior hands to check difficult rigging.
Her household has **grown children** and roughly three months of expenses saved, so she needs paid work while retirement approaches.
She will use **proven fault tools** but insists on signed isolation records and a human safety check at the pole.
The **2031 robot date** worries her most; longer runways let her verify retirement income, save modestly and seek inspection work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable repair robots follow in 2031, before she can build much more savings.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written staffing plan**, paid inspection training and a reliable estimate of retirement income.
